speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
that Bill S-17, an Act to amend the Copyright Act, the Industrial Design Act, the Integrated Circuit Topography Act, the Patent Act, the Trade-marks Act and other acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when my colleague in the opposition applauds, that is a good sign; it means that this is a good bill. I want to thank him for that. You will also allow me to thank the senators who studied this bill and passed it.
Government Orders
I believe this is the first time that Parliament has considered a bill amending five laws on intellectual property. This is a first for the Parliament of Canada. I think that several departments should consider such an approach so that, where a vast subject is concerned, the laws dealing with it can be improved together as a package.
Bill S-17 is a result of consultations with the interested community and those concerned are in favour of the various amendments contained in the bill. One may wonder why we would amend five laws on intellectual property all together. For one thing, it is to make the system more efficient and, for another, to make it more accessible for Canadians.
With this package, we are making administrative and technical changes to five existing laws. In the world economy as we know it and as it is coming to be, no country will be able to live or survive if it does not look after developments related to intellectual property. Any country that did not consider intellectual property a priority would be mistaken. In this regard, we in Canada have been working and must continue to work.
The various pieces of legislation we are discussing today are not necessarily up to date and do not necessarily meet the needs of Canadians, which creates higher costs for Canadians in the intellectual property sector who use these five different acts.
I can give some examples of how the situation has changed. Take the Patent Act, for instance. Today, according to the legislation, an inventor must provide a detailed description of his invention in writing, but we know that in 1993 and future years, there will be many new developments in biotechnology. Describing an innovation in biotechnology in writing is probably not the best and cheapest approach for most users. Producing a sample of the biological material would be a more sensible and practical alternative, and that is one of the changes we find in Bill S-17.
Electronic filing and processing of all patent-related documents does not exist at the present time. This is something else that has to be done, both for the government and for Canadians who use the system. Technically, a person can now file a new application but

March 16, 1993
Government Orders
not be able to protect an existing application. Some technical amendments are therefore necessary. One can easily imagine the problems and inequities this can create, so these are the kinds of amendments being proposed in Bill S-17. Of course, filing of patent applications will be simplified.
With regard to the Trade-marks Act, since 1954 there have been no technical or administrative changes in this legislation. We know that today, for instance, it contains no definition of an entity, but it does contain a definition of a group. Once again, these matters are dealt with in the bill.
Bill S-17 also provides for improving the operation and administration of the Copyright Office. Canadians will have better services.
Earlier we referred to the Industrial Design Act. It is important to protect our industrial designers. As you know, Mr. Speaker, although the Industrial Design Act has been in existence for almost a century, there have been no significant amendments to improve the legislation in many years, so this is important. I may add that all the amendments mentioned were suggested and approved by people in this sector.
At this point I would like to congratulate the Intellectual Property Advisory Committee, which was created in 1988, on its excellent work. Committee members represented business, cultural groups, consumers, universities, researchers and experts.
Lawyers.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
My honourable friend mentioned lawyers, but I wanted to use the word "experts". In any case, we understand each other. It boils down to the same thing.
These are people who worked very hard to make changes and provide positive and badly needed solutions for the intellectual property sector which was covered by five different acts.
Finally, this legislation, which is intended to improve the administration of five acts, will simplify procedures. It will simplify the technical aspects and introduce advanced technology, while giving Canadians more convenient access to the intellectual property sector.
The Senate has already examined the bill and judged it to be a valid piece of legislation.
I hope my colleagues on the other side of the House will adopt this legislation as soon as possible. If they are prepared to adopt all stages of the bill today, I am available. I would be delighted to be here in the House to support the bill and ensure it is adopted without further delay.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate the hon. minister on his ascension into glory with his new position in the cabinet. I have had the pleasure of working with him in the House since I was elected and so far he has been a refreshing change from the way that some things work around here. We have already had a few meetings and they have been somewhat productive. I think this is the first bill that the minister has introduced in the House, and so it is a milestone for him. It is generally a good bill to be introducing.
I say that because of the process that resulted in this particular piece of legislation coming before this place. For those who are watching, it happened in kind of a strange way. Bill S-17 was not initiated in this place but in the Senate, or the other place as we call it from time to time. It was introduced in the Senate of Canada. This is the reversible pipeline of legislation which we do not see a lot of in Canada. Indeed, it was debated, there was some committee study, and witnesses were heard.
It comes to us now after having had a fairly significant degree of examination and after some witnesses have come forward. It is sort of a hodgepodge and does a whole lot of things. There are five acts dealing with intellectual property which it proposes to amend. This bill came up through an advisory committee of stakeholders in the industry which had been set up. It went through a lot of the issues of the day dealing with intellectual property in Canada and the things it could agree on it did. It came forward with a series of amendments to five acts.
The five acts are the Copyright Act, the Industrial Design Act, the Integrated Circuit Topography Act, the Patent Act and the Trade-marks Act. Many parts of this bill deal primarily with housekeeping and try to harmonize regulations and correct some deficiencies and prob-
March 16, 1993

lems that the industry stakeholders have had some level of consensus on.
I am not about to say at this point in time that I think that type of approach has led to a flawed bill. That is the way we should be approaching legislation in the House of Commons. If we had more legislation coming forward after that type of non-combative and non-partisan review and consensus we would have better legislation on the floor of the House of Commons.
If we go back to Bill C-22, the Bankruptcy Act, my colleagues on all sides of the House had an unprecedented level of agreement when we pre-studied the bill. Then when we returned to the partisanship, after approval at second reading, things started to come apart again.
There was something that told us way back then that we could do legislation differently. When we consult widely and listen to people's points of views the Canadian people are the ones who benefit because we have better legislation. We are able to strip away a lot of the nonsense that goes on here from time to time and we are able to tap into the intellect, experience and commitment of all members of Parliament, and it does not really matter whether they are Tories, Liberals, Reformers, Bloc Quebecois or New Democrats. Most people who come to this place come here because they want to serve the public of Canada.
I know that the minister was quite anxious to try to get this bill through the House today because of the factors I have just mentioned and because it has already had some debate in the other place. We have not agreed to do that, not because we want to hold the bill up but for two reasons.
First, I am a firm believer that we are paid to oversee the passage of legislation. Although I have a great deal of respect for my colleagues in the other place I was not over there when this bill was debated.
I have read the committee reports and I have perused the Hansards from the Senate. Nevertheless, this is a fairly complex bill. It has over 70 clauses in it. Much of it is highly technical.
For me to say today that I trust what has gone on in the other place, and there do not appear to be many flaws
Government Orders
with the bill, so let us just get it through to clear the legislative agenda is not in the service of Parliament. It does not pay the deserved respect to the people who have put this legislation together.
As a purist, I believe that we have to go through the process and I think we will be doing that over the next few days.
The second problem I have is that there are a number of places in the summary where it says that certain clauses in the legislation have the effect of giving Governor in Council more regulatory authority. In short, in these cases it says, and it may be for good reason, that we will give the Governor in Council, which is the executive branch, the right to change certain aspects of the implementation of these pieces of legislation solely by regulation.
When we deal with regulation, then I have some trouble with that. The former minister knows this. When we are dealing with regulation we owe it to the people of Canada to be very sure that we understand the full impact and the depth of the regulatory powers we are giving to bureaucrats, who after all are not accountable, do not have to face the electorate, and are not public figures.
In this bill, and I guess we will find this out in committee, there are a couple of clauses that bother me more than a little. One is clause 8, which amends the Copyright Act. It allows the Governor in Council, which is the executive, to change the fee structure for the application process for copyright by regulation. That bothers me, because I have always felt that any fee that is imposed, be it a user fee, an application fee or a direct piece of tax legislation, is a tax. Any time we are talking about giving unelected people the right to go forward and alter fees without any debate in this place and without going back to a parliamentary committee I get a little nervous. Perhaps when we get to committee we will be able to talk to the officials and find out exactly what regulation-making powers we are giving to them.
There is one other aspect of the bill that bothers me, and it deals with the patent co-operation treaty. I will be quite honest. I am not exactly sure what the heck it is all about. One thing that does bother me is that one clause of the legislation which would change the way we do things quite clearly gives Governor in Council the ability to pass regulations that can override the legislation. That

March 16, 1993
Government Orders
seems really strange to me, and I am not exactly sure how that is done. I would strongly doubt, unless we are just giving very limited powers, that is the type of precedent we would want to be pursuing. We will be asking questions again on that particular aspect of the bill.
There is another aspect of the bill which I have a little difficulty with, and it concerns biological deposits. This is a whole new field for us, in which new pharmaceuticals, new strains of crops and things like that are coming forward, and it is based on biological agents. My concern is only that we should explore this more closely. We have to look at exactly what we are doing.
In the past, from what I can gather from reading the summaries on the legislation, many times a biological sample would be deposited as part of the application process and they would say that this is a sample of what is and it is different from anything before, so they would ask us to give them a patent on it. That has not been accepted in the past and there have been some court cases on that issue.
My concern is that this now makes that biological deposit acceptable as a significant body of evidence to justify the granting of a patent. I am not opposed to it, but I am concerned about its retroactivity. I am not convinced from the information I have read that it is clear. What would happen if a patent had been struck down, or if a patent had been rejected based on the fact that the main supporting documentation for uniqueness was the biological deposit, or the sample, which was not accepted before?
If there is product out there now and this bill has some retroactive impact, what happens to a farmer who has a particular strain of hybrid seed for which he was never able to get a patent in the past? What happens to some of the drugs and pharmaceuticals currently out there? Indeed, there are a number of pharmaceuticals in the field which may now be challenged by some of the generic companies as to the validity of the patents. I want to find out what will happen to those court proceedings or those cases if they do go forward, if this bill is passed.
In conclusion, we are looking forward to some discussion on this bill when it does go to a legislative committee. Our intention certainly is not to hold it up. I applaud the process by which the bill came forward.
The stakeholders in the industry have waited a long time to get these things cleared up and have done an exemplary job so far. I would just ask them to wait a little bit. We have a few questions from our end. Perhaps working together we can come up with a piece of legislation we can all be proud of and that will fix some of the problems dealing with intellectual property in those five various fields.

Mr. Speaker, when dealing with Bill S-17 we have to also deal with the fact that this bill before us has been presented to us in a very hasty manner from the time it was initially presented in the other place.
We have not really been adequately briefed. We have not been briefed at all by the government which is presenting the bill. Furthermore, this is a bill if ever there was a bill that needed to go to committee for a thorough analysis to look at the consequences in many areas. On religious grounds, people could be veiy much opposed to the genetic engineering aspect, the biotechnology aspect of this bill. This kind of bill needs that airing out in a committee with expert witnesses.
Very quickly I am going to go over what this bill does and does not do. Generally I think it is safe to say that this is a hardware bill. It is a house cleaning bill which is being put forth by the government in order to bring many of the related laws we already have on intellectual property into line and make them applicable in a most efficient manner.
For the people who are watching and listening to us today I want to mention that on intellectual property we are basically dealing with patents. We are dealing with creators of functional ideas. We are dealing with much more than books. We are dealing with medicines, biotechnology, the creation of completely new organisms. Some very serious questions arise from the impact of this legislation.
As my colleague has said, without opposing the government's Bill S-17 we could still have a better idea on how to actually be in favour of it if we could get a full airing out of its implications and particularly the retroactivity aspect of parts of the bill.
March 16, 1993

The bill essentially makes amendments to five different statutes all dealing with various aspects of intellectual property. Patents, which protect the embodiment of ideas of a functional nature, are governed by the Patent Act. Copyright, which protects the expression of ideas, is governed by the Copyright Act. Trade marks, which protect symbols and distinguished goods and services in the marketplace, are regulated by the Trademarks Act. Industrial designs, which relate pretty much to ornamentation applied to an article, are governed by the Industrial Design Act.
An interesting new field is called topographies. As a new MP I remember asking: What is this bill on topographies? What are we talking about? I was thinking of territory, topography on a map. That is not what it means at all. My friends, here we are dealing with the computer age. We are dealing with microchips. This is called topographies, or the contents of a microchip. That is actually regulated by-and here is that word again- the Integrated Circuit Topography Act. If that word is seen in the newspaper, they are talking about microchips.
All that is what Bill S-17 is concerned with. It is important to highlight that this bill was not sneaked in. Although it has been very hastily presented to us, it was not sneaked in. This bill was not bull-dozed. The bill has had extensive consultation and hearings with different consumer groups. Actually, the Canadian Bar Association was one of the players as well.
The bill has been involved in a great deal of consultation. All we are asking as members of Parliament is that the consultation continue in committee so that we can understand the full intent of this legislation before we adopt it.
The amendments to the Copyright Act are primarily of an administrative nature. For example, it eliminates the requirement that entries in the copyright register be personally signed by the registrar of copyright or by the commissioner of patents. That sounds to me to be a fair housekeeping measure.
Dealing with the Industrial Design Act the bill allows the applicant to designate somebody else, an assignee to file an application in their own name. You can designate someone to make an application. Once again that seems to be a fairly inoffensive part of the bill.
Government Orders
With respect to the Integrated Circuit Topography Act this would extend protection to us and countries which are reciprocating with Canada. That is just common sense to me.
I have some serious misgivings when it comes to the biotech part of this bill where we are dealing with new organisms. I am not quite sure that it cannot be described in writing. As a writer myself I would like to know why we would be going against the recent ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada which said it had to be in writing in order for it to be valid when application was made for a patent.
I understand the biological sample can be deposited and that would be the example. That would be your so-called application part of the affidavit, but I am not quite sure that in and of itself would suffice. There should be some attempt to write what went into that biological sample, why it is so unique and why there should be a patent on it.
Dealing with this whole question of biogenetic engineering, I am very much concerned that we are actually homogenizing life forms. We are homogenizing plants. We are homogenizing animals. If you read the papers, it appears we are creating a new strain of pig so that we can have parts for transplants.
I am concerned that this is something that is going to receive a great deal of scrutiny by the churches and by people with religious beliefs who do not believe we should be involved in this. He who controls the patents for seeds, animals and livestock, what does that do for the agricultural sector where farmers with the ability wish to buy these animals and seeds without having to deal with a monopoly of a company? It may be a pharmaceutical company or some other company which has a patent on that particular livestock or that particular seed. I am wondering about that. That question has to be answered in committee.
Finally when talking about biogenetics and talking about creating new organisms we are really talking about getting a patent on life. To claim a patent on a life form is a direct and total denial of that person above looking down upon us who is the ultimate individual, I believe, to have that right. We have to look at the whole question of what creation means and whether we can actually seek a patent on creating new life forms.

March 16, 1993
Private Members' Business
There are serious questions that we have to deal with in committee. However, I do applaud the minister's approach. I think it is salutary for the House to present a bill in this way. I hope for a speedy passage of it in committee.

Mr. Speaker, just by way of background, I compliment my colleague again for having the foresight to bring what I call the accountability and reliability of taxation measures before the House of Commons by way of a private member's bill.
On the last day we spoke on this legislation we were discussing in some detail the effects that legislation like this would have.
Suffice it for me to say that this legislation would make all government programs to be costed out fully and completely before any programs were implemented. Any cost overruns would need the special authorization of Parliament. That really is the critical issue with respect to this legislation.
Even if this House were to approve some project, once that project exceeded the approved limitations of this House, the legislation would have to reappear before the House of Commons. Every member would be apprised of the efficiency of that project. Then there would be a debate on the full extent of the additional costs involved in any program the government implemented.
It would require long-term planning by cabinet ministers. They would have to give the House a very detailed statement on the original cost of the program, the cost in the previous two years and the expected cost over the next five years.
The last time we were debating this particular legislation I made a statement with respect to the goods and services tax. Let me use the goods and services tax as an example of what this legislation is all about. When it was implemented there was some accountability with respect to what it was supposed to do on the taxation system in Canada.
We heard many statements on what was the original start up cost on the goods and services tax. The estimate we heard at the time was that with the addition of 4,000 employees by Revenue Canada in order to monitor and police the goods and services tax, the start-up costs in implementing this tax were going to be $1 billion.
That $1 billion was only an estimate. The tax has been in effect for some two years. We still do not know how much revenue that tax has generated to pay off our debt. We heard at one time that when comparing the goods and services tax with the manufacturers' sales tax which it replaced, that it was going to be revenue neutral. We still have not heard. We have had no accountability from the government with respect to whether the goods and services tax is revenue neutral as it said.
What is the net revenue of the goods and services tax with respect to how it affects the total debt of this country? What are the original set-up costs? To this date we do not have the figures with respect to the actual
March 16, 1993

start-up cost of the goods and services tax. It is information I think all Canadians want to know.
What are the effects and how much money has been reimbursed to all Canadians since the start up of the goods and services tax? I speak of the amount of money that was being sent back to those taxpayers in Canada under the poverty line who could not afford to pay the goods and services tax and were to be reimbursed for the added expense to their cost of living. To this day we have not been apprised of that particular figure. We are interested to know.
The manufacturers' sales tax was reduced. We want to know how much was reimbursed to all the manufacturers and retailers who were compensated for the inventories they had in so far as the manufacturing tax was concerned. How long did that manufacturing tax stay reduced or removed from the products they were selling? What is the experience of those products with respect to increases in prices?
We talk about exports. Canada is a great exporting country, but we have not found out yet how much money is returned to manufacturing industries in Canada that pay export tax on their production methods. When they export those goods to other countries, how much is reimbursed to manufacturers in Canada in businesses entirely involved with export? That is remuneration every member of this House should have knowledge of so we can assess fully the accountability of the government with respect to how much it cost to implement the goods and services tax.
Another example and one that is very prevalent today is that of the helicopters. We talk about accountability of the government. When the helicopters were first introduced in Canada they were supposed to be $2.8 billion. I see the Minister of National Defence who originally gave the contract out is with us today. It was $4.4 billion. We have just heard in the last two months that the contract was no longer $4.4 billion but had risen to $5.8 billion. The legislation my friend is trying to implement and put forward by way of a private member's bill is the means by which this House can control that type of expenditure.
I know my time now has elapsed but I compliment him for having the foresight to bring forth this type of legislation which is so badly needed by this government and by future governments of Canada to control expenditures and save the taxpayers of the country the money

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague for Kent for bringing forward this private member's bill. It must be a pretty good bill when some people want to address it twice or more. It requires a bit of persistence on the part of a private member and a bit of luck too to get a private member's
bill this far. I want to congratulate my colleague from Kent county.
This bill has a reputation now for being what we call a common sense bill. That in itself is a rather simplistic way of describing something, but it has a lot of common sense and sensibility about it although it is officially called an act to amend the Financial Administration Act.
A few parts of it sort of fascinated me. We can put them in more complicated context if we like, but what would be wrong with having a bill that would very simply state the objectives of any program? That would seem to make sense to me. One of the objectives of my colleague's bill, Bill C-301, would be to state clearly the objectives of the program.
Another would be the estimated total cost of the program over its proposed life and the method by which that cost would be estimated. How do they determine that cost? Unless we know that, they may have forgotten to build in some of the factors which would have a bearing on the final cost of the project. Then there are the estimated sums that will be required for the program over each of the first five years. Sometimes several things we have noticed in this House have come in as what they call cost overruns.
Let us sit down and determine every five years whether a program is still accomplishing what its original objectives were. Is the estimated cost so far out of whack that if we had had all that information initially we would no longer have the program, for example? It would not seem to be anything but common sense to me to anticipate some of those things and evaluate them every five years.
The anticipated effects of the program on the economy, environment, employment and social programs in Canada tend to change periodically. An ongoing evaluation of a program every five years would seem to be in keeping with what we are endeavouring to do.
Finally there is the appropriation out of which the program will be funded. Where is the money going to come from for this program?
I noticed the Minister of Finance made a statement as reported in The Ottawa Sun of February 10.1 could table
March 16, 1993

it if anyone is interested. I just want to read a short paragraph which states: "The federal deficit of $34.4 billion is still a big problem". That is what the Minister of Finance said. "He admitted it particularly with the figures released yesterday showing the deficit widened in December to $1.74 billion from $1.54 billion a year earlier".
With my colleague's bill that sort of thing would be less likely to happen. It would not guarantee that it could not happen. However if it started to happen we would have the mechanism in place where we could say: "Let us examine it, let us put it under the microscope, let's see if its original objectives are still valid and do something about it instead of just lumbering on".
The impression in the general public these days is that government spending, not only federal but provincial and I suppose municipal too, is out of control. Reducing the annual deficits in my opinion is the only way to address the long-term debt. If we do not attack the annual deficits how are we ever going to be in a position to attack the long-term debt?
If someone thinks this bill is too risky maybe it is time the federal government and all other levels of government started to take those risks. I do not see it, for example, threatening long-term strategies and longterm plans. Perhaps it would cause us to examine those long-term strategies and those long-term plans, something we have been rather reluctant to want to do.
The public from its point of view sees paying more, paying more and paying more and getting less, getting less and getting less at the same time in which the deficit keeps mounting. That is rather puzzling for the public. It seems this bill would be an attempt to try to get a hold on things so that would not happen, so that would not be allowed to happen.
The idea of cost overruns really means being accountable to the public every once in a while so that there would not be cost overruns and some of the things the Minister of Finance said in The Ottawa Sun on February 10 would be less likely to happen. The other thing the public is continually saying, to me anyway, is: "If we ran our businesses the way that you guys spend our money, we would be out of business very, very quickly.

There is great evidence of that. In this country in 1992, 76,139 people declared bankruptcy. They were not allowed to carry on any further. Somebody put a stop to it. The government does not seem to be in any position, seemingly, to realize that that could happen to the government. More and more regularly you are seeing that there is a great threat. If independent businesses can declare and have to declare bankruptcy, put in a position where they must declare bankruptcy, perhaps it would not be so unusual for the government to visualize the difficulty that the public has in seeing from their perspective why governments are allowed to go on when they have been put to the point where they have had to declare bankruptcy and are out of business.
It is this government's ability, it seems, to disregard all the rules under which private enterprises and private businesses must operate that is aggravating the people. That is why there is so much cynicism today and so much concern about the debt that this country is carrying.
As we all know, it is very easy to get into debt but it is sometimes very, very difficult to get out of it. There are times, of course, where it would make sense to get into debt, but I think what has happened in relation to government is that it does not seem to have a plan for getting out of debt. If you are going to get into debt you should have some plan for getting out of debt.
I think my colleague's bill here is a modest attempt at trying to be realistic about getting into debt. Some kind of an ongoing evaluation must be in place to see that you have a plan for getting out of debt. Only in government are you allowed it seems to get into debt without having any realistic plan for realizing that there will come a day when you must concern yourself with getting out of debt.
Governments do not do things very efficiently. My opinion on that is perhaps it is time they started to do things more efficiently. The reason they do not do things efficiently is because they have never had to. They have got into the habit of thinking that there is a bottomless pit there and all they have to do is tap it and it continues to fill up, something like a spring I guess, once you tap it there is a source there of unending wealth.

March 16, 1993
Private Members' Business
We are now in debt in this country to the tune of about $450 billion and it is growing by the minute. I think that is what my colleague's bill is attempting to address, to see if something could be put in place, something in the way of a common sense bill which would allow governments, indeed force governments to have a process for regular examination. Hopefully, that would avoid the cost overruns which get us into the problems that have put us into the $450 billion debt category.
It does not mean that programs would cease by any means. It means that there would be more scrutiny applied whenever a new program was introduced. I congratulate my colleague on bringing this bill forward. I for one will have no hesitation, and I hope those on all sides of the House will see the sense in supporting this bill. I wish him the very best when the vote is taken, if it gets that far.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today also in support of the motion presented to the House by the hon. member for Kent. I think it has been described as the common sense motion. I would suspect that government members if they were not government members but sitting on this side of the House would be voting in favour of it today. It seems to me that what I am hearing from opposition members and as I read some of the speeches from past Hansards and some of the speeches that have been given on this bill, they are things that I have heard members of the Conservative Party speak about when they were in opposition. It is unfortunate that they lost this part of their rhetoric when they made the transition from opposition into government.
.(1725)
They were quite eloquent at times in opposition when they talked about Parliament losing control over spending, that spending was out of control, that we needed a new system and a much tighter system of accountability in order to get spending under control.
I read the remarks from the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State for finance and the excuses he was giving us today. If I would have had the time I would have gone back through the records because I am certain there is a speech somewhere before 1984 where that hon. member would have made remarks in this House criticizing the
way expenditures occur and the lack of control over them.
Our country is facing very serious financial problems. We have growing deficits adding up to a horrendous debt that will take generations to pay off. It is time we got our house in order. It is time we stopped allowing expenditures to occur that get out of control.
There is one megaproject after another. Estimates come in, the House approves certain expenditures, a month later we hear that the expenditures have gone up. One, two, three or five years later when the final bill comes in, we begin to realize that it is nowhere near what the original estimate was, what the original approval was for.
It is time for that type of activity to come to an end. We cannot continue to afford that type of expenditure. When the minister or the government make proposals for certain expenditures, those proposals should have a total scrutiny so that Parliament knows if the estimates are accurate, if there is inflation built in and what the final bill will be. Not only Parliament but the people of Canada should know.
As members of Parliament we are ultimately responsible. It is not the government, it is this House of Commons. Ultimately, we the members of this House of Commons are responsible for the type of debt and deficit that we are facing now.
As members of Parliament we are not given the opportunity nor the information to really make wise decisions. In part the government and the bureaucracy want to maintain this control. That is why I believe we now see- Conservative members who truly should be supporting this bill speaking against it because they are now captured by the government and not acting on what they really believe in. Surely they really believe in trying to control government expenditures so that we have wise expenditures and members of Parliament can fulfil their proper duty.
The other thing that appeals to me was expressed as I read the remarks of the hon. member for Kent when he moved a motion in the House. If I may quote from his remarks that appeared in Hansard, Monday, November 30, 1992: "As well any cost overruns would need special authorization. It requires long-term planning by cabinet ministers. They would be forced to present to Parliament a detailed report showing any program's cost and its
March 16, 1993

effects on the economy, environment, employment and social programs to the extent that it is possible".
This House has fruitfully debated the whole notion of environmental review so that governments, particularly governments but also private industry, cannot engage in massive undertakings that would alter the physical environment of our country, alter the quality of air or water and affect living species, et cetera.
Now we demand that there should be an environmental review so we know the environmental costs to a program. I maintain we also need a social environmental review. We know when unemployment goes up and poverty goes up, crime, suicides, violence and drug and alcohol dependency go up. There are social costs to this government's Unemployment Insurance Act that it is presenting to Parliament.
Social scientists can show the statistics, the correlation between an act of this government that would restrict the number of people who are eligible to receive unemployment insurance for example and the social effect that will have. They can predict with a relative amount of accuracy the number of suicides, the number of crimes, the amount of family breakdowns, and violence that will occur.
The hon. member suggests in this bill that we should also have some social cost accounting so that when government brings in measures Parliament also knows the effects they will have on our community, on the people and the cost to treat the social ills that a certain particular measure the government might introduce might create.
I think there is a lot of common sense in this bill. I suspect that government members in their hearts would likely want to support this bill. I urge them to let their hearts speak and not their blind ambition of trying to get a cabinet position at some stage.
This bill calls for the government to be more accountable to Parliament in its expenditures. What is the problem with that? Why are Conservative members opposed to that? Is this not really a conservative philosophy that is being introduced here?
As a New Democrat I have no trouble with that. I believe as my colleagues believe, and I am sure hon. members across the way believe, that the government
Private Members' Business
has got to be accountable to Parliament. No greater area for accountability is there than accountability over expenditures and how the government spends the taxpayers' money.
That is what is being called for in this private member's bill. It deserves the unanimous support of this House.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Kent for introducing this private members' bill, one of the very few private member's bills which is votable. I apologize for cutting off the hon. member for Burlington but I did not want people who have not spoken on the bill to lose their time on it.
The media has already dubbed this bill as a common sense bill which I think is the intent of this bill and that is to put curbs on runaway government spending.
CFCO radio in the hon. member's riding said this about the bill. "What Crawford's bill proposes is that government be responsible with our money, that spending is studied before it is done, and overspending be answered for. His bill would give more people in Ottawa a kick at the can known as accountability, members of Parliament, the Auditor General, and the Standing Committee on Public Accounts".
That pretty well sums up the intent of this bill. We have been hearing a lot in Question Period and in debates recently in this House about the cost of the Cadillac helicopters. Initially when the purchase of the helicopters was announced the tab was $4.2 billion. Now all of a sudden it has jumped up to $5.8 billion and the taxpayers are fed up with that kind of throwing taxpayers' money into the wind.
Be honest with taxpayers and tell them exactly what the cost will be three years from now, five years from now, or ten years from now.
We have an experience right in Toronto, a project near my riding of Parkdale-High Park, the SkyDome. In 1985 when the SkyDome project was proposed the cost of the SkyDome was $150 million.
Everyone thought this was a great project that would bring in jobs and revenues. The public was sold on it, but by the time the contract was signed in April 1986 the figure had jumped to $234.7 million. Once all the final

March 16, 1993
Private Members' Business
touches were put on the Sky Dome, the final cost was $590 million.
Three levels of government were involved as well as taxpayers. I support the Sky Dome. I think it is worth every dollar of the $590 million, but the planners and designers should have been honest with the public and said: "The cost of the Sky Dome will be $590 million". They should not have jumped from $150 million to $590 million.
I am looking more specifically at clause 3 of the bill and part III.I, which deals with the creation of new programs. It says that where a new program is to be established requiring the expenditure of money appropriated from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, the minister who is to be responsible for the administration of the program shall, prior to the commencement of the fiscal year in which the program is to be continued or established, lay before Parliament a statement showing the objectives of the program. It should show the estimated total cost of the program over its proposed life; the method by which the cost has been estimated; the estimated sums that will be required for the program over each of the first five years; the anticipated effects of the program on the economy, environment, employment and social programs in Canada; the appropriation out of which the program will be funded.
Section 42.2 deals with the excess costs. Where the minister is informed that the cost of a program on which he has laid a statement before Parliament pursuant to section 42.1 will exceed the estimated cost shown in the statement for any year, the minister shall lay before Parliament a statement showing the amount of the excess cost for the year, the reasons for the excess and the alternatives that have been considered before concluding that the excess is unavoidable.
Looking at the bill in detail, I think it ensures that the taxpayers' money is wisely spent through good planning. The bill ensures that taxpayers' money is protected because controls will be in place to do proper accounting.
The bill ensures that taxpayers' money is not wasted through over-costing and if more money is needed for the completion of a project, justification must be given for the additional money required.
I am appealing to the members on the government side and I am pleased that the hon. member from Burlington South has spoken on this bill. He did say that this bill flies in the face of parliamentary tradition. It would threaten the ability of governments to plan strategically. It would cloud the services of the Auditor General who should not be a commentator on government long-term objectives.
I think just the opposite. I think this bill would help government plan strategically and help the Auditor General do his job.
The member went on to say he did not think requirements should be invoked which inhibit the government's ability to govern effectively. The government is governing ineffectively now and that is why the hon. member for Kent brought in this bill. This would allow governments, present and future, to plan more effectively.
The member from Burlington South went on to say the government will want to consider whether the proposed amendments are in the best interests of the House. I was never aware that the legislation we pass here is for the best interests of the serving members.
I think the legislation we bring and pass in this House should be measured by whether it is in the best interests of the people who elected us. Is the legislation we pass in the best interests of the taxpayers who are paying for these projects and programs, such as the constituent who called me just before this debate? She is a single parent with a child to raise. She earns $26,000 a year and cannot make ends meet. There is the small business entrepreneur who has to pay the GST and it is killing the business. Whatever legislation we pass should be in their best interests and not work against their best interests as some of the present programs this government has brought in are doing.
I am again appealing to the government members to support this bill. I know some members look at things very objectively and listen to their constituents, as the hon. member for Kent has. I know my constituents support this bill 100 per cent. What the hon. member heard from his constituents I am hearing from my constituents in Parkdale-High Park. They are just fed up with overspending.
March 16, 1993

I might remind the members that once this bill is voted on it is passed to the committee. Sure it needs a lot of fine tuning, but the committee can do that. Let us not kill a good thing here.
I hear a lot of bellyaching on this Hill, Mr. Speaker, as you do, about members wanting more freedom to vote on legislation that reflects the wishes of their constituents. Here is an excellent example. If we have any guts, and I am speaking to members from all parties and the independent members, let us show that we can do things constructively. We do not have to listen to our leaders on this bill. We do not have to listen to the Whips on this bill. We have to listen to our common sense because this is a common sense bill. If we vote for it we have done the right thing in this House once and for all by listening to our constituents. Therefore I encourage every member in this House to be on his or her feet supporting this bill as soon as we have the vote.
I believe that I have 10 minutes, Mr. Speaker. Is that the case?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: You have up to 10 minutes.

I will not take much time, Mr. Speaker. I simply want to mention that what my colleague from Toronto just said is true. As usual, he made some good points and I fully agree with him.

I would like to take perhaps a different tact to what has been taken until now. I would just like to focus the members' attention on a program you may have seen, Mr. Speaker, about a week and a half ago about New Zealand. A number of people have spoken to me about it and I suspect they have spoken to other members here as well.
Let us just look at three themes struck in the CTV W5 program. During 1984, the year foreigners simply stopped buying New Zealand government bonds, all levels of government deficit in New Zealand were at 7 per cent of its GDP. The accumulated government debt in our sister member of the Commonwealth that year was 62.7 per cent of its GDP. Its net public-private
Private Members' Business
foreign debt, according to W5 at least, was 47 per cent of its GDP.
If you fast forward to our country in 1993, the yearly budget deficit for all levels of government for 1992 was
8.5	per cent of our GDP. Our accumulated all-government debt, which is approximately $650 billion I believe, was 90 per cent of our GDP. Our net foreign debt of approximately $300 billion was 44 per cent of our GDP.
I would ask hon. members if anyone in this House thinks that federal-provincial budgets will get better during the current calendar year.
The music stopped for New Zealand's financial party in 1984, the week the newly elected Labour government of David Lange learned its central bank lacked enough foreign currency to meet bond interest payments. A very excruciatingly painful crackdown on government spending followed immediately because, as former Prime Minister Lange put it, his government was "suddenly forced to behave like it was to the right of Genghis Khan". Over the next decade, New Zealanders watched their standard of living drop from third to twenty-second in the industrialized world. A final point on that program is that the New Zealand politicians of all stripes agree that excessive government deficits did them in.
Richard Prebble, Labour associate minister of defence between 1984 and 1989, said: "More debt is like liquor to an alcoholic. Governments must bite the bullet". The current New Zealand health minister, Simon Upton of the National Party, added: "We had hit our credit limits. The only difference between Third World states and countries like New Zealand and Canada is that we are given more rope to hang ourselves with".
Does anyone in this House disagree? Do we really think as members of this House that the IMF is very far now from Canada's financial doors? Does anyone in the House think our country is going to avoid the New Zealand wringer if we continue to spend and borrow, the spend and borrow addiction of the Mulroney years and, in fairness, some earlier Liberal ones?
Our federal-provincial finances are simply grotesque by any objective measurement. How can any MP or MLA for that matter-and I know we prefer to blame the voters for asking for more and more government servi-

March 16, 1993
Private Members' Business
ces-look any young Canadian in the eye today? Do Canadian politicians have no responsibility to avoid putting the standard of living of our children and grandchildren at risk? If they knew what our collective profligacy had done to their futures, I think they would want to run us out of every capital across this land.
Premier Clyde Wells put this point very well the other day. He pointed out that in 1975 each Canadian family's share of the national mortgage so to speak was about $50,000. In 1993 it is about $665,000.
The problem, as some members will appreciate, is that a new government, hopefully a Chretien government, will be caught between a very fragile economic recovery and escalating federal-provincial debt. Too much cutting too fast would cause our economy to shrink yet again, taking many real family incomes even further downward and increasing UI and other social spending, thereby ultimately adding to federal and provincial deficits.
That said, I am very proud of my leader for saying no to the purchase of 50 submarine-chasing helicopters, the price of which has already jumped from $4.4 billion to $5.8 billion even though the jobs, to put it mildly, would not be created proportionately across the country.
And most of them not even in the country.

Indeed. I guess I will leave it there. There may be other speakers. I simply want to say that I hope all hon. members in this House will respect the McGrath committee and will vote according to their consciences, not according to what their party Whips tell them to do on this important vote. We can do ourselves proud, I think all of us, by voting for it.

Mr. Speaker, I commend my colleague from Kent on his thoughtful approach to a reasonable bill that would bring a great deal of credibility to this House of Commons, if this bill were passed.
We are talking about credibility. If we stop and think about a small service organization, if we stop and think about every municipal government whether it be the city of Toronto or the small town of Harrow, we know that planning for the future is done through a budget process where all people elected to office are carrying out very
diligent views of what is happening within that budget process. This bill is basically asking for that budget process to be dealt with on a reasonable basis.
As a member of the House of Commons one of the things I find very difficult is the fact that I do not have access to the knowledge about how money is being spent in the government. I do not have the information I need to direct my constituents about federal spending. It has been the case ever since being elected. Projects are announced in my riding. I tried to get detailed information about those projects and it was not available to me.
One of the examples that I could give is a project that was announced in Wheatley, in my riding, a $1.5 million marina project. I went to the estimates and searched through them to try to find where that $1.5 million was tucked into the government estimates or accounts so I could make sure that this money had been put aside for that project.
I went through it in as much detail as I could. An expenditure the size of $1.5 million did not appear. It was announced during the election. A large sign was erected in the town of Wheatley, saying "$1.5 million for a marina to be constructed here." However, that money was not placed in the estimates. It was not placed where the general public or a member of this House of Commons could have found it.
Pursuing through the bureaucracy to try to find where those dollars were spent and how those dollars could be brought to Wheatley, I could find no record anywhere. I could not find a department that could say that money had been placed there. This is four years later, and that has not been spent. The sign was placed there saying that this project would go ahead but it is not there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 27 last year I raised a question with the Minister of the Environment concerning assistance from the federal government to the area of Victoria with regard to the sewage treatment problems it is having.
As it considers this issue the House should first understand that over one thousand communities in Canada dump raw sewage into Canada's lakes, rivers and streams. Unfortunately Victoria is not alone, although we are probably alone in the international abuse we are taking for the problem. In this we feel very much aggrieved.
We have tried hard to deal with the sewage treatment problems in our area. We have a new collector system. We have a modern screening system. We are taking the advice of engineers on how best to dispose of our sewage.
As the House may know, although many members will not have an acute grasp of the sewage problems of Victoria, the system the engineers have recommended would take the sewage well out into the straits of Juan de Fuca where the waters are cold and quickly moving. The engineers tell us, though most of us as lay people find it impossible to understand and believe, that it is quickly
Adjournment Debate
absorbed into the water and is of very little serious consequence to the environment.
Be that as it may, we in Victoria are determined to deal with this problem. It has given us international difficulties. The member opposite who will be replying for the government seems to smile at this. It is not a happy problem for the people of Victoria, and I suggest for the people of Canada, because of the consequences. Conventions have been cancelled because of this problem. We think it is an unfair rap because we have tried.
We look to the federal government for support in two areas. The first area is the problem of communicating the facts about the efforts that are happening in Victoria to our friends, particularly in the United States, who are being encouraged not to understand this issue as it should be understood. Instead of laughing at us, I would hope that the government would be sympathetic with us on this issue and would help us with a communications strategy.
Second, I would hope that the government would be prepared to sit down with the provincial government, the capital regional district and the local municipalities to determine if we can actually come up with a more effective method of treating our sewage. In our community on the whole we simply do not accept the engineers' advice. We would like to see better sewage treatment than we are getting.
We have to continue to deal with the other environmental problems in our community including how to get rid of liquid waste and solid waste. We are trying to do that, but it would be helpful if the government would be prepared not just to try to sell us some surplus land, which was the government's most recent offer, but to constructively sit down and help.
The federal government provided $200 million to Halifax to help it with its sewage treatment. So far the government has not put up one dollar to help the people of Victoria. I hope the government will take this problem seriously, as we do, and assist us in dealing with this very difficult environmental problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 6 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member opposite that the minister stated back on November 27 when the member asked his question that the municipal waste water discharge is an

March 16, 1993
Adjournment Debate
environmental issue that needs to be addressed. British Columbia's ministry of the environment, lands and parks is now taking a very strong stand with respect to municipal waste treatment in British Columbia and is requiring that all municipalities move toward secondary treatment systems.
The hon. member for Victoria made specific reference to the situation in Victoria. Let me assure all members of the Elouse that this government is committed to encouraging the provision of the necessary sewage treatment system in Victoria.
The federal government's goal is to promote a sound approach to management of municipal waste waters. The federal approach is built on its role related to technological development and transfer to promote the optimization of municipal treatment facilities, public education about water use and responsible decision making, the use of economic instruments such as full-cost pricing to provide adequate funding for municipal infrastructure requirements, environmental stewardship to ensure that federal waste waters are dealt with in an environmentally sustainable manner, and the development of a better scientific understanding of the environmental impacts.
I am sure that the member for Victoria is well aware that the federal government is in the midst of intensive discussions and negotiations with the capital regional district of Victoria and the province of British Columbia concerning the treatment of Victoria's sewage, and progress is being made. Given the position being taken by the province, we remain very optimistic that a negotiated agreement can be reached and that the city of Victoria will soon be developing plans, obtaining land, confirming funding, and beginning construction of appropriate sewage treatment facilities.
As part of this government's leadership in promoting sustainable development the polluter-pay principle has been adopted in decision making on environmental issues. As the municipal and provincial governments have the primary responsibility for the management of municipal waste waters and treatment infrastructures, we recommend to the responsible authorities the use of economic instruments such as user fees in addressing this issue.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 26, prior to the finance minister's economic statement, I asked in this Elouse whether his forecast would be accurate and reliable with respect to the deficit. As well, I asked whether he would put forward measures to create jobs now for our unemployed. The finance minister answered that his statement would give encouragement, optimism and hope for the future.
Surprise, surprise. It certainly did not do that. Instead, the finance minister presented a stay-the-course budget with more cutbacks and more attacks on the jobless, recipients of unemployment insurance, and public servants. Besides failing to stimulate the economy, Canadians were faced with higher unemployment into the future.
As if this were not enough, the finance minister had to admit in his economic statement that this government has been unable to deal effectively with its pet economic cause, which is the deficit. The finance minister admitted in his economic statement that the deficit for this year would actually be $7 billion higher than he had predicted the previous year, and that it would be $10 billion higher the following year.
I wonder today whether even those predictions are false because I gather that the deficit will be even higher. It might be as much as $8 billion higher than he had predicted.
It is three months later, and we are asking the same questions. The finance minister in previous years said that this Conservative government was absolutely going to give us a budget every year at the same time in February. Of course, it forgot to say that it would not do it in 1993.
Then we had the scenario of the off again, on again budget. First he was going to give us a budget some time toward the summer, but then we were not sure because he was not sure whether he was going to run for the leadership or not. Now I gather we are going to have a budget after the Easter break.
I am going to ask again if the government is prepared to listen to Canadians. Canadians really need hope. More and more are joining the ranks of discouraged Canadians.
March 16, 1993

We can quote statistics and can talk about fundamentals, but when I am in my riding office person after person comes to me saying: "What am I going to do?
I do not have a job. I want a job. I want to work". Other people are telling me that they are worried whether they will have their jobs next month.
What will the government do to provide some hope? Is it possible or is it absolutely impossible? Has this government totally lost touch with the realities of Canadian life?
It is absolutely essential first, to have the kinds of forecasts we can rely on and, second, to give some hope to Canadians by creating some jobs right away, not sitting there, doing nothing and waiting for something miraculous to happen and then maybe there will be jobs for Canadians.
Once again I ask that the government give Canadians, not just me, the replies and actions they have been awaiting for some time now.

Mr. Speaker, the member for Sudbury asked if the government would present a deficit forecast in the economic statement. As she already knows, the government has presented its new deficit forecasts: $34.4 billion this year and $32.6 billion in 1993-94.
The member will have noticed that the deficit outlook for this year and next has deteriorated essentially because of the drop in revenue due to the slow recovery of the Canadian economy from the 1990-91 recession.
The member says that Canadians want jobs. I wholeheartedly agree with her on that. But what does she recommend? Maybe a magic economic formula? Of course Canadians want jobs. Perhaps the member would like to use a magic wand to create them. The Canadian economy was slowed down by a world-wide economic crisis. Just wishing that it were not so and that everyone had jobs will not make our problems disappear. Much as the member might want it to be so, the Canadian economy cannot be the little engine that will pull the world economy out of its slump.
Adjournment Debate
The government's economic strategy is to invest in growth. Sound budgetary and monetary policies, streamlining the machinery of government, freer trade and broader opportunities for business have created an economic environment favourable to the private sector. This is the sector which holds our potential for future growth.
By investing in Canadians acquiring skills, we have a more productive labour force and more competitive producers. More funds are being given to manpower training programs. Investing in human resources will ensure the basis for lasting improvements to our prosperity.
Small businesses create the most new jobs in this country. The government has helped them with various tax breaks and incentives for research and development. The government is proposing an exemption for unemployment insurance premiums to small businesses that create more jobs next year. It is proposing a 10 per cent investment tax credit and raising the limit for loans to small businesses.

Mr. Speaker, as I said in the House of Commons last November, I was astounded to hear that the NDP's interim waste authority had included site M-6 which borders on the Rouge River Valley on the short list.
I went on to say that if the NDP government were foolish enough to proceed with this site, my government would seriously consider terminating the $10 million financial commitment we made in 1988 to help create a natural heritage park in the Rouge Valley.
In mid-January the NDP government approved a plan to create the natural heritage park which will be 20,000 acres in size or 26 times the size of Toronto's High Park. This news while late in coming is wonderful. What is far from wonderful is that the IWA is still considering M-6 as a possible site for metro Toronto's 40 million tonnes of garbage. When we made the $10 million commitment for the park it was conditional on three critical elements: no dump, no roads and no housing in close proximity.
I have talked to the federal Minister of the Environment and he is very concerned and disappointed that a

March 16, 1993
Adjournment Debate
megadump is still being considered on site M-6. It is simply too close to the proposed park.
Just today I heard that the IWA had drilled seven test holes on the site and it expected this step to be finished by the end of March. Anne Katsoras who chairs the citizens' advisory committee against the dump told me today about that news and said the community was working hard to organize several events to help raise community involvement and awareness of the seriousness of the M-6 site proposal and to help raise money.
The NDP government continues to ignore considering viable options such as incineration or the rail haul option to the Adams mine site near Kirkland Lake.
Provincial Bill 143 forbids consideration of all other options. Landfill is the only option to be considered. It restricts the area for the megadump. It says metro Toronto's garbage must be dumped in York region. It could not, for example, be dumped one-half mile outside York region. This is crazy.
The NPD government continues to close its eyes and ears to the views of the people of this province. We will not forget or forgive it for this arrogance and insensitivity. There will be an election in two or three years. As I have said in my December 1993 mailing to 52,000 residents of Markham-Whitchurch-Stouffville: "We will throw Bob Rae and Ruth Grier out of office before we allow a shovel in the ground at M-6".
Bud Wildman was recently appointed minister of energy and environment and Ruth Grier was shifted to the health portfolio. Howard Hampton became minister of natural resources. We would think that these new ministers might have taken a new look at the absolute havoc bill 143 will create in Ontario.
Regrettably they have missed this opportunity. They are still marching blindly to Bob Rae's band which is determined to wreck this once great province with regressive tax measures, harmful labour laws and outlandish spending resulting in horrific deficits, to say nothing about Bill 143, one of the most undemocratic laws I have ever seen.
If the Rae government would simply listen to the people and the facts it would have another good reason to forget about the M-6 site. One reason concerns Transport Canada and its bird hazard guidelines published in 1989. These guidelines stated that a dump site
could not be created within an eight-kilometre radius of an airport or a heliport. The M-6 site is only three kilometres from the heliport at Markham-Whitchurch-Stouffville hospital. This is a 24-hour emergency service. The M-6 site is also less than eight kilometres from the Markham airport and is only 2.5 kilometres from the edge of a potential international airport on the Pickering lands.
The Minister of State for Transport has also expressed her amazement that the Rae government would ignore the guidelines and therefore put people's lives at risk since air crashes are a distinct possibility when there are thousands of sea-gulls at a megadump.
In closing I want to say again that I will do everything I can to stop Bob Rae and the IWA from creating a megadump at the M-6 site. I cannot believe they would be so stupid to proceed with M-6.
In the end we may have to drag this issue into the courts for two or three years, by which time there will be an election and we can throw the rascals out along with the IWA.

Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member on his perseverance in the situation in the Rouge Valley.
The IWA or the Interim Waste Authority was established by the Government of Ontario to examine and review all potential landfill sites within the regions of Durham, Peel and York metro. The members of the advisory board are charged with making a single recommendation for a landfill site in each area by mid-1993.
The inventory of the potential sites was based on scientific and technical data rather than on political and social pressures or considerations. That is the over-all game plan of the Ontario government. It functions at arm's length from the Government of Ontario and its recommendations reflect the members' technical assessment and not the government's plans or policies.
The IWA has reduced its long list of 50 sites down to a short list which still includes M-6, an area bordering on the Rouge Valley. Consequently M-6 will be assessed in terms of its technical feasibility. Adjacent land use and other influencing factors will be weighed accordingly when its suitability is being considered.
March 16, 1993

Subsequent to the IWA final recommendations, public hearings will be held to encourage input and inquiry into the appropriateness of the recommended sites following the consultation stage. The final decision will still rest with the Ontario cabinet.
In all likelihood the next stage of technical assessment will eliminate M-6 from the short list. As IWA operates independent of the government's proposed plans for land use in the Rouge Valley and as the government's current support for a park in the Rouge Valley neither restricts nor encourages the IWA's review process, advising the Ontario government of the federal government's concerns would not prove effective at this time.
The minister of natural resources made the Government of Ontario's position quite clear on January 19 of this year when he announced the creation of an urban park within the Rouge Valley and the preservation of
8,000	acres of adjacent agriculture land. The M-6 site is located within the area identified for preservation as agriculture land.
In evaluating the suitability of M-6, the IWA will now have to take into consideration the Ontario government's expressed intention to establish a park in the Rouge Valley. It is a decision which will likely have considerable influence in the IWA's final assessment of M-6 suitability for landfill purposes.
I remain confident in the Ontario government's commitment to the Rouge Valley park. I am hopeful that the IWA recommendations will not favour the M-6 site, given its current and projected adjacent land use.

Mr. Speaker, on December 1 last year, I asked a question in the House about federal funding for the fight against the AIDS epidemic. I asked the government to accept the unanimous recommendations made by the four main groups that are fighting against AIDS in Canada: the Canadian AIDS Society, the Canadian HIV Research
Adjournment Debate
Foundation, the Canadian Hemophilia Society; and the Canadian Public Health Association.
Last week, these four associations and all Canadians received the government's response. It was negative.

The response of the Conservative government was a devastating blow to those involved on the front lines in the fight against AIDS.
Instead of the budget of $55.35 million per year which was requested as a minimum by the four groups to which I have just referred as well as by the ad hoc parliamentary committee on AIDS in a strong and unanimous recommendation to the government, the Minister of National Health and Welfare allocated $42 million a year. This falls far short of what is essential in the fight against AIDS. Tragically we will, of course, spend more money later rather than now on prevention and on assisting community groups that are on the front lines of the struggle against this epidemic.
I want to ask the parliamentary secretary to the minister for an explanation as to why this government ignored the recommendations of the four national groups that are on the front lines in the fight against AIDS as well as the ad hoc parliamentary committee. Why did it ignore these recommendations?
Government says it does not have enough money for the fight against AIDS. At the same time it is prepared to spend $5.8 billion on attack helicopters. This government is morally and ethically bankrupt.
On the same day I asked the government when it was finally going to keep the promise to amend the Canadian Human Rights Act to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation.
Over seven years ago, seven long years, the Minister of Justice of the Conservative government promised to accept the unanimous recommendation of the equality rights committee and to amend legislation federally to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation.
The Ontario Court of Appeal said that the federal government's law was unconstitutional, that it violated the charter of rights. How did the minister respond? The then Minister of Justice is now the Minister of National Defence. She wants to be leader of the Conservative Party. She said: "Well, okay. I will bring in an amendment to include sexual orientation". However, in the same breath she brought forward an amendment that denied the reality of gay and lesbian relationships. It

March 16, 1993
Adjournment Debate
restricted the definition of those relationships and restricted the definition of marital status to opposite sex relationships.
That is not only an attack on committed loving relationships, but it also flies in the face of the Leshner decision of the Ontario Human Rights Tribunal. It flies in the face of the very eloquent comments of Madam Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dube when she spoke in the judgment in Mossop on the reality of Canadian families.
I call upon the government to bring forward the necessary and long overdue amendments to ensure full equality and justice for lesbians and gay men in this country, but not to take away a fundamental element of that equality by defining marital status in the narrow and restrictive way that the Minister of Justice did.
In conclusion, I once again appeal to the government to increase the level of funding for the epidemic against AIDS and to amend Canadian human rights legislation to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and also to recognize the reality of lesbian and gay relationships in that act and in all other federal legislation.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 6 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the hon. member for Burnaby-Kings-way, on March 11, 1993 my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, announced that the government would renew the national AIDS strategy.
The renewal of this strategy for a period of five years, at a time of severe financial cutbacks, is an indication of the federal government's commitment to meeting the challenge of fighting AIDS and HIV-related diseases. The national AIDS strategy, phase two, will receive
annual funding totalling $42.2 million, or $211 million over the next five years. This new funding represents an increase over the annual $37.3 million provided in phase one.
At a time when federal departments are being asked to downsize their programs, this investment in the health of Canadians is tangible proof that the federal government is committed to finding a cure for this disease.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has also asked his deputy minister to provide an annual supplement of $1.5 million from his department to improve support for initiatives in this area.
Furthermore, the Medical Research Council of Canada is committed to spending $2 million annually over the next five years to support AIDS research. Since 1983, the Council has spent more than $13 million on research and education in this field.
That is why I appeal to all Canadians to get involved and support what is being done by the government, community groups, researchers, health professionals and the private sector.
As the minister has said repeatedly in the House and on many other occasions, this government remains firmly committed, now and in the future, to the objectives of the national AIDS strategy.
In concluding I would like to add that I think the national AIDS strategy is an indication of this government's commitment to improving its social policy and making Canada a healthy country.
